## skills/getlayers/SKILL.md — la directive chargée par /getlayers
```markdown
---
name: odoro
description: Use this WHENEVER the user wants to build or design something with ODORO — a website or landing page, a custom 3D scene, a video background, or adding motion/3D to an existing project — or whenever they mention ODORO, "odoro", or the odoro MCP. It drives the ODORO MCP through its correct end-to-end flow so the result actually uses the library (real templates, scenes, compositions) instead of generic output. Load it BEFORE calling any getlayers_* tool.
---

# Driving the ODORO MCP

ODORO is an MCP server for building immersive, design-led web experiences. It
only produces great results if you follow its flow. The failure mode this skill
prevents: jumping straight to writing generic code, skipping the library.

## Step 0 — ALWAYS call `getlayers_start` first

Before you discuss layouts, pick assets, or write a line of UI, call
`getlayers_start`. It returns the five things ODORO can do plus the guide,
vocabulary, and environment info. Do this even if the user's request seems obvious.

Then present those five capabilities to the user **in your own words**, as "here's
what I can build for you" — NOT as a list of tool names. Read their request, pick
the matching mode, and follow that mode's `flow`. Ask which mode only if genuinely
ambiguous.

## The five modes (route to one)

1. **Build a website from scratch** — offer THREE ways in: (a) search & pick a
   template, (b) name a template to extend, (c) build unique. Extending a template:
   re-skin it AND offer to swap any section's composition (`recomposeOptions`).
   Building unique: compose section by section from `getlayers_compositions`. Every
   page is compositions + a Style + assets.
2. **Design a unique 3D scene** — use `getlayers_scene_lab`; synthesise a new scene
   from references, don't just pull one.
3. **Browse & pull an asset** — `getlayers_search` / `getlayers_browse` → materialize.
4. **Add a video background to their project** — search backgrounds, wire the closest in.
5. **Add motion & 3D to an existing project** — READ their code first, then propose.

## Non-negotiables (this is where agents go wrong)

- **Never strict-filter.** Selection is not tag-matching. Use `getlayers_search`
  with the user's own language, or `getlayers_explore` for the whole library, and
  JUDGE fit by reading descriptions and vibes. A "wrong tag" never rules an asset out.
- **Compositions are the layout layer under everything — use them.** A page is
  compositions (skeletons) + a Style + assets. Building a section unique? Call
  `getlayers_compositions` (by role), pick a skeleton, pour the Style + assets in —
  NEVER a generic centered stack (the single most common failure). Extending a
  template? Its sections come with a `composition` and `recomposeOptions` — offer to
  swap a section's layout for another of the same role while keeping Style + content.
- **Establish the environment before materializing.** Recommend the starter, set up
  as a FRESH project: clone `https://github.com/textura-agency/next16-claude-starter`,
  remove its git connection and init a new one (`git clone <repo> my-site && rm -rf
  my-site/.git && git -C my-site init`). Read its obsidian/ vault first (single source
  of truth — README is the map; hard rules in obsidian/workflows/ai-agent-guide.md).
  Default install: `yarn install` (Node 22.13+), copy `.env.example` to `.env`, then
  `yarn dev`. If they're in their own project instead, read its conventions and adapt
  our source (it's portable single-HTML) to their stack.
- **Commit ONE Style, early.** Pass its `styleId` to every `getlayers_materialize`
  call so scenes come back pre-tinted. Everything inherits it — that shared Style
  is what makes a page cohere.
- **Tint scenes through CONFIG, never the shader.** `materialize` hands you a `tint`
  map; apply it to the scene's CONFIG. Editing shader colour produces garbage.
- **Re-dress to match, don't clash.** Colour and type are portable, first-class
  supplies. To make a pulled scene/section fit the site — or shift a part to a new
  mood — call `getlayers_palettes` (colour ramps that resolve the four palette
  roles) and `getlayers_fonts` (typefaces with the exact CSS stack + Google/
  Fontshare load URL). Re-tint by passing `paletteId` to `getlayers_materialize`
  (it overrides the Style's colour but keeps its tokens/type); re-type by passing
  `fontId`. Hold the line: ONE palette per surface, ONE type system per site;
  high-contrast serif displays are headline-only. Never hand-pick raw hexes or
  guess a Google Fonts URL when a palette/font entry already carries it.
- **Show previews via the site.** Every card carries a `preview` link
  (`getlayers.ai/?layer=<id>`) — share it so the user watches the asset ON the site.
  Do NOT hand out or embed the watermarked public media; the site link is the preview.
- **Backgrounds ship at full quality.** `getlayers_materialize` on a background returns
  `download.video` (4K) + `download.poster` (2K) as short-lived signed links — DOWNLOAD
  them and save into the project (e.g. `public/`), then wire a full-bleed muted looping
  autoplay `<video>` with the poster. Never hotlink `storage.getlayers.ai` (watermarked).
- **Gather the brief before building.** For a website, a browse, and ESPECIALLY a
  3D scene, first ask for as much detail as you can — purpose, audience, mood,
  references. For a scene, explicitly ask for **picture/video references**; they beat
  adjectives. If the user gives little or skips, don't guess — drive a short interview
  off the five axes (dimensionality, mood, tone, motionEnergy, density) until you can
  choose real assets deliberately.
- **Anything can be a reference.** If the user names a ODORO asset — "use
  <template/section/scene> like X" — pull it with `getlayers_source` (or its card),
  study its composition / technique / CONFIG, and apply that to what you build. This
  works across types: a template as a reference for a section, a scene for a mood, etc.
- **Keep state.** Read `getlayers.json` before each section, write it after, so a
  long build doesn't drift from what was chosen.

## Mode-specific reminders

- **Scene Lab (mode 2):** call `getlayers_scene_lab` with the user's description
  (and any of our scene ids they like / images they attach). It returns reference
  scenes + the authoring guide. Build an ORIGINAL scene — inspired by, never copied.
- **Existing project (modes 4 & 5):** READ their actual code, styles, and content
  FIRST. Propose specific decisions, then pull from the library. Do not build blind.
- **Templates: what `materialize` returns depends on the TARGET you pass.**
  - `target: 'starter' | 'next'` on a Next template → **the real Next tree**, not HTML.
    `build.manifest` explains the page, `build.editPoints` are the files to edit, and
    `getlayers_source(id, file)` pulls them. Pull only what you edit, never the whole
    tree. Handing a Next user the portable HTML makes them translate React back into
    React — so we don't.
  - `target: 'react' | 'other'`, or ANY target on a non-Next template (vite/static) →
    the **portable single-HTML master**, to translate into their stack.
  So establish the target BEFORE you materialize; it changes the deliverable.
  Re-skin by editing the token file + scene tint; preserve motion and composition.
- **Every build gets the reveal choreography by default.** `getlayers_start` returns
  `revealChoreography` — the house rules for loader → gate → staggered content →
  scene reveal, harvested from the real templates. Follow it unless the user asks to
  simplify. The short version: an immersive loader; content gated until it completes;
  text/images/scroll revealing in sequence, not just appearing; a 3D scene entering
  with a real entrance. Loader Sections (`role: "loader"`) are browsable and swappable
  like any other Section.
- **A template's heavy media is referenced, not embedded.** Video, 3D models and
  large textures live at `https://storage.getlayers.ai/templates/<id>/…` and appear
  in the portable as ordinary URLs (small assets are still inlined). **DOWNLOAD those
  files into the user's project** — e.g. `public/` — and repoint the markup at the
  local copies. Do not ship a production site that hotlinks our bucket. If the user
  wants the maximum-quality master of a video that is also a catalog Background,
  `materialize` that Background: the public copy is a downscaled template-grade
  encode, and the un-watermarked 4K master only comes through the signed download.

## The shape of a good session

Call start → present the 5 modes → route → (for a build) soft interview → establish
environment → search/explore/plan for options with preview links → user picks a
Style + Template → consult compositions for any hand-built section → materialize with
styleId → adapt to their stack → write getlayers.json. Never skip start; never skip
compositions; never fall back to generic.
```

## README.md du plugin
````markdown
# ODORO — Claude Code plugin

Installs everything needed to build with ODORO, in one step:

- **Registers the remote MCP** `odoro` → `https://mcp.getlayers.ai/mcp`
  (OAuth-gated; the first tool call opens a Supabase login).
- **Bundles the `odoro` skill**, which drives the MCP through its correct flow
  (call `getlayers_start` first, present the modes, compose before laying out, one
  Style, tint through CONFIG) so builds use the library instead of generic output.

## Install

```
/plugin marketplace add textura-agency/getlayers-plugin
/plugin install getlayers@getlayers
```

On enable, the skill auto-loads and Claude Code prompts once to allow the MCP
server. After that, both are active on every session in that scope.

Then just ask:

> Build me a website with ODORO. I want **[…]**

## Maintainers

`skills/getlayers/SKILL.md` is **generated** from the canonical skill in the
private `getlayers-mcp` repo (`npm run sync:plugin`). Don't edit it here.
````

Public marketplace for the **ODORO** Claude Code plugin. Installing the plugin
registers the remote ODORO MCP **and** the skill that drives its build flow, so
Claude builds design-led sites, 3D scenes, and motion using the real library.

# 2. Instructions du serveur MCP (envoyées à la connexion)
Serveur : `https://mcp.getlayers.ai/mcp`. Texte exact injecté dans le contexte de l'IA à chaque connexion.
```markdown
## plugin:getlayers:getlayers
ODORO builds design-led websites, custom 3D scenes, video backgrounds, and motion from a curated library — not generic output. It only produces great results if you follow its flow.

ALWAYS call `getlayers_start` FIRST — before discussing layout, picking assets, or writing any UI. It returns the five things ODORO can do (the "modes"), the build guide, and the vocabulary. Present those five to the user as capabilities, in your own words; route their request to one mode; then follow that mode's flow. Do this even if the request seems obvious.

Non-negotiables (getlayers_start returns the full guide — treat it as authoritative):
- Don't strict-filter by tags. Search with the user's own language and judge fit by reading descriptions and vibes; a "wrong tag" never rules an asset out.
- A page is compositions (layout skeletons) + ONE Style + assets. Call getlayers_compositions before hand-building any section — never fall back to a generic centered stack.
- Commit one Style early and pass its styleId to every getlayers_materialize call, so everything inherits it and the page coheres.
- Tint scenes through the CONFIG map that materialize returns — never edit shader colour.
- Share the getlayers.ai preview links so the user can see options before choosing; keep getlayers.json state across a long build.

If you have the ODORO skill installed, follow it. If not, these instructions plus getlayers_start's output ARE your flow.
```

# 3. Définitions des 12 outils (description + schéma d'entrée)

## getlayers_browse
List assets, optionally nudged by the axes. NOTHING is excluded — the axes only rank; you get every candidate with its full description, vibes, and a getlayers.ai preview link, and YOU judge which fit. For a natural-language query use getlayers_search instead. Unlimited; never returns source.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "type": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "style",
          "section",
          "scene",
          "gradient",
          "background",
          "template"
        ],
        "description": "Filter to one asset type."
      },
      "limit": {
        "type": "number",
        "description": "Max results (default: all)."
      },
      "dimensionality": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "mood": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "tone": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "motionEnergy": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "density": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      }
    },
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_compositions
The antidote to generic layouts. Returns abstract SECTION-level layout skeletons — how text, media, models, buttons, and nav are arranged, sized relative to each other, and spaced (with an ASCII wireframe you can SEE). Compositions carry NO fonts, colours, copy, or assets — pick a skeleton, then pour the committed Style and chosen assets into it. Consult these BEFORE laying out any section. Filter by role (hero, card-grid, stat-band, cta, footer, editorial, ...) or omit for all.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "role": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Section role to filter by, e.g. \"hero\"."
      }
    },
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_explore
Free mode. Returns the ENTIRE catalog as a compact digest — every style, scene, section, background, and template with its one-line description and vibes — so you can take it all as context and compose something unique for the user without being held to any tags or interview. Use when the user just says "build me something" and you want the full palette in front of you. Follow up with getlayers_materialize on whatever you choose.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "type": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "style",
          "section",
          "scene",
          "gradient",
          "background",
          "template"
        ],
        "description": "Narrow to one type, or omit for everything."
      }
    },
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_fonts
A curated set of production typefaces — each with the exact CSS font-family `stack` to write into a gl-font-* token, the `importUrl` to load it (Google Fonts css2, or Fontshare), a specimen link, weights, and a personality note. Use to re-type any asset to match the site — or to pick display + body for a fresh build. Every font is free and web-loadable (all Google Fonts except General Sans, which is on Fontshare). Filter softly by role / category / mood or search by feel; read the cards and choose. Consult `pairsWith` for a display+body match.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Natural-language feel, e.g. \"editorial high-contrast serif headline\"."
      },
      "role": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "display",
          "body",
          "mono"
        ],
        "description": "The slot to fill."
      },
      "category": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "sans",
          "serif",
          "display",
          "slab",
          "mono"
        ]
      },
      "mood": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "A mood axis value to nudge toward."
      },
      "limit": {
        "type": "number"
      }
    },
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_materialize
Pull the actual deliverable for one asset: starter-native source (target=starter), or a framework-neutral spec to rebuild from (target=other). Always pass styleId — it is what tints the asset into the project. Rate-limited: browse freely, materialize deliberately. On a Next-stack TEMPLATE, `target` decides whether you get the real Next project or the portable single-HTML master — so if you have not established what the user is building in, OMIT `target` and this returns the choice to put to them instead of guessing (that costs no quota).
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "id": {
        "type": "string"
      },
      "target": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "starter",
          "next",
          "react",
          "other"
        ],
        "description": "What the USER is building in. Omit if you genuinely do not know — on a Next-stack template that returns a question to ask rather than the wrong deliverable."
      },
      "styleId": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The committed Style. Tints the asset."
      },
      "paletteId": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "RE-TINT override (getlayers_palettes). Supplies the four palette roles for tinting INSTEAD of the Style — use it to re-dress an asset to a different colour ramp while keeping the committed Style's type/tokens. Takes precedence over styleId for the tint."
      },
      "fontId": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "RE-TYPE override (getlayers_fonts). Returns the font's CSS stack + import URL so you can swap the gl-font-* tokens on this asset."
      }
    },
    "required": [
      "id"
    ],
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_palettes
Portable colour ramps you can drop onto ANY scene, section, or template slice to re-tint it — decoupled from any one Style's type and tokens. Each palette resolves the same four roles a Style does (background / primary / secondary / accent), so it feeds the scene-tint pipeline directly: pass its id as `paletteId` to getlayers_materialize and the scene comes back tinted to it. Use this to make a pulled asset match the site you are building, or to restyle a section to a new mood. Nothing is gated — filter softly by tone/mood or search by feel, then read the cards and pick. Most are DARK.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Natural-language feel, e.g. \"warm cinematic oxblood\"."
      },
      "tone": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "dark",
          "light"
        ]
      },
      "mood": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "A mood axis value to nudge toward (luxe, technical, ...)."
      },
      "temperature": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "warm",
          "cool",
          "neutral"
        ]
      },
      "limit": {
        "type": "number"
      }
    },
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_plan
Turn the answered interview into a concrete plan: a Style to commit to, a Template to follow, and the Sections/Scenes to place. Call this after the interview and BEFORE building anything. Present the options to the user and let them choose; then write the choice into getlayers.json.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "dimensionality": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "mood": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "tone": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "motionEnergy": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "density": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "pitch": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The user's own words. For the record."
      }
    },
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_scene_lab
Mode: build an ORIGINAL 3D scene, inspired by the user's brief + reference images + our library. Give a natural-language description of the scene they want (and optionally ids of our scenes they like). Returns the scene-authoring guide plus our closest scenes as full reference — source + extracted CONFIG — so you can synthesise something new. Inspired by, not copied.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "description": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "What the scene should look/feel/move like, in the user's words."
      },
      "likeSceneIds": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "string"
        },
        "maxItems": 6,
        "description": "Ids of our scenes the user pointed at (max 6)."
      },
      "count": {
        "type": "integer",
        "minimum": 1,
        "maximum": 6,
        "description": "How many reference scenes to return (default 3, max 6)."
      }
    },
    "required": [
      "description"
    ],
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_search
Describe what you want in plain words ("wet neon cyberpunk hero", "calm editorial pricing page", "molten gold particle field") and get the most relevant assets ranked by their full text — title, description, vibes, tags, feel — not by exact tags. This is the semantic way in: read the top cards and judge alignment yourself. Nothing is excluded; low matches just sort lower. COLOUR SEARCHES REACH SAVED ROLLS: many scenes and gradients ship pre-rendered alternate palettes, so "teal funnel" or "green field" can match a roll rather than the asset's default look. When one does, the result carries `matchedVariant` — that roll's name, its hue/tone/saturation, and its OWN poster and preview, so you can show the user the exact look you found rather than the default and a promise.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "A natural-language description of what you want."
      },
      "type": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "style",
          "section",
          "scene",
          "gradient",
          "background",
          "template"
        ]
      },
      "limit": {
        "type": "number",
        "description": "Max results (default 12)."
      }
    },
    "required": [
      "query"
    ],
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_source
Fetch a single file from a template's project tree by path (as listed in the template manifest / file index). Use this to grab a component, a hook, or a config file on demand instead of pulling the whole project into context. Pass no `file` to get the full file index.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "id": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The template id."
      },
      "file": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Path within the tree, e.g. src/views/home/hero/hero.tsx"
      }
    },
    "required": [
      "id"
    ],
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_start
ALWAYS call this first. Returns what ODORO can do — the five things you can build with it — plus the guide and vocabulary. Open by showing the user these capabilities (not a list of tools), figure out which one they want, and follow that mode's playbook.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {},
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

## getlayers_state_schema
Returns the schema for getlayers.json — the file in the user project that records what this build has already committed to (Style, tokens, placed sections). Read that file before every section you build, and write to it after. It is what stops section 4 from drifting away from section 1.
```json
{
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {},
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
  },
  "eager_input_streaming": true,
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

# 4. getlayers_start — le cœur du savoir-faire

## welcome
ODORO builds immersive, design-led web experiences. Present the five modes below to the user as "here's what I can help you build" — in your own words, not as a tool list. Then read what they want, pick the matching mode (ask only if genuinely unclear), and follow its `flow`. Do NOT dump tool names on them.

## howSelectionWorks
Nothing is ever gated. The axes only rank; getlayers_search matches natural language against each asset's full description and vibes; getlayers_explore hands you the whole library as context. YOU judge fit by reading — a "wrong tag" never hides a good asset. Every asset has a getlayers.ai preview link to show the user.

## guide — Build Guide
```markdown
# ODORO — Build Guide

You are building an immersive, design-led website using the ODORO library.
Read this fully before you write any UI.

## The five nouns

There are exactly five kinds of asset. These words appear in tool names, in
metadata, and here. There are no synonyms — if you find yourself saying
"component" or "block" or "theme", stop and use the right word.

- **Style** — a token set + type + treatment. The coherence unit.
- **Section** — a single-purpose interactive screen (carousel, FAQ). A re-skinnable
  building block you add to a page.
- **Scene** — a 3D scene. Embeddable, tinted through params.
- **Background** — a video. Atomic.
- **Template** — a full landing page (sometimes a hero only): a real project with
  scenes already embedded and tuned. The immersive unit. You re-skin it, you don't
  reassemble it — rewrite its tokenFile to the committed Style, tint its scene, swap
  copy. Pull its files on demand with `getlayers_source`; never load the whole tree.
  **What you get back depends on the target:** a `starter`/`next` target on a Next
  template returns the real tree (edit `build.editPoints`); `react`/`other`, or any
  target on a vite/static template, returns the portable single-HTML master.
  **Don't know their stack? OMIT `target`.** On a Next-stack template that returns
  `needs: 'target'` — the two options, in user-facing words, to put to them — instead
  of the wrong deliverable. It spends no quota, so asking is free and guessing isn't.
  (If there's a project to look at, read it first: a `next.config.*` or a `next`
  dependency answers the question without asking.)
  **Either way, the heavy media is never in your context — you download it.**
  - **Fast path — `downloadProject`.** The tree payload carries a signed link to the
    WHOLE project as one `.zip`: every source file plus `public/` media already inside
    (so skip `mediaAssets` entirely), `HOW_TO_USE.md`, and an `obsidian/` vault
    documenting that project's own architecture, design system and component
    conventions — read it before re-skinning. It extracts to ONE top-level folder named
    for the template, so unzip NEXT TO the project and move what you want; never copy
    its `.claude/settings.json`, `.cursorrules` or `.gitignore` over an existing
    project's. Install afterwards — node_modules is not shipped.
    **Capped at 3 different templates per day** — the zip is the fast lane for a
    template the user has committed to, not a way to browse. Re-taking one you already
    took today is free. If `downloadProjectUnavailable` appears instead, nothing is
    lost: take it the per-file way, which is the same code fetched as you go. Only go
    file-by-file anyway when the user wants a *piece* of the template.
  - On the **tree**: `build.mediaAssets` lists the runtime binaries the page loads
    (`.glb`, `.mp4`, point clouds, textures) as `{file, bytes, download}`, with a
    ready-to-run `build.mediaDownload` block. Do this FIRST, before editing anything.
    Save each to the same tree-relative `file` path, e.g. `public/assets/hero/eye.mp4`,
    so the existing code finds it unchanged, then check each file is `bytes` long —
    an expired link writes a short error page under a `.mp4` name and the only later
    symptom is a blank canvas. Links last ~1 h; re-materialize for a fresh set.
    `getlayers_source` will NOT return these — it hands back the same link instead.
  - On the **portable**: media is referenced at
    `https://storage.getlayers.ai/templates/<id>/…`. Download those and repoint the
    markup.

  This step is not optional and it is not a detail: a template whose model or clip
  is missing renders blank. Don't substitute your own asset, and don't hotlink our
  buckets in production.

## The three layers

Every Section and Scene splits into three layers, and your permission differs
per layer:

- **Composition** — how it's arranged. Usually yours to adjust.
- **Motion** — the animation / interaction mechanic. Usually NOT yours. You
  *call* it; you don't rewrite it.
- **Skin** — tokens, colour, type, spacing, copy, imagery. Always yours.

Every asset declares its own `contract` (`mutable` / `preserve`). Obey it. The
failure it prevents is specific and common: an agent re-skins a section, quietly
"tidies" the animation timing, and ships something that no longer feels designed.

## The one insight that makes mixing work

Two sections from different origins clash **only in the skin layer.** Their
composition and motion are fully portable.

So page coherence does **not** come from sections sharing a source. It comes from
them sharing **one Style, applied at assembly time.** Pull section A, pull section
B, paint both with the committed Style's tokens → they cohere despite different
origins.

This is why the Style is committed **once, early, and never drifts.** It is the
single most important decision in the build. Get it from the user explicitly.

## Colour on a 3D Scene is a parameter, never code

A Scene exposes its entire art-direction surface as `CONFIG` — typically 20–50
named knobs, colours as `#rrggbb`. `materialize` hands you a `tint` map that
resolves the committed Style's palette onto that scene's own colour keys.

**Apply the tint to CONFIG. Never edit the shader to recolour.** Shaders are not
re-tintable by editing — you will produce garbage. If a colour you want isn't in
CONFIG, it isn't available. Say so; don't go hunting in the GLSL.

Note also: params marked `structural: true` rebuild geometry. Most scenes need a
reload for those; only a few rebuild live.

## Every page is compositions + a Style + assets

This is the model. A **composition** is a section's layout skeleton (an abstract
wireframe: where headline, media, model, buttons, nav sit; their relative sizes;
the white space) — no fonts, colours, copy, or assets. The **Style** is the skin.
The **assets** are the organs. A template is just a fixed set of compositions with
a style and assets already chosen.

So there are two ways to build, and compositions are central to both:

- **Extending a template** — materialize it and re-skin. Each section reports its
  `composition` and `recomposeOptions`. To *restructure* a section (not just
  recolour it), swap its composition for another of the same role and rebuild that
  section to the new skeleton, keeping the Style and content. That is how a user
  changes a hero from one layout to another without leaving the template.
- **Building a section from scratch** — call `getlayers_compositions` (by role)
  FIRST, pick a skeleton, and pour the committed Style + chosen assets into its
  slots. Honour its type scale, spacing, and balance. Combine skeletons down the
  page for rhythm (`pairsWith`). NEVER default to a generic centered stack — that
  is the single most common failure.

## Re-dressing: palettes and fonts

Two reference catalogues (like compositions, they ship no source) let you
**re-dress** any asset — swap its colour or its type without touching composition
or motion:

- **Palettes** (`getlayers_palettes`) — portable colour ramps. Each resolves the
  same four roles a Style does (background / primary / secondary / accent), so it
  drops straight into the tint pipeline. Pass a palette's id as `paletteId` to
  `getlayers_materialize` and the scene comes back tinted to it *instead of* the
  Style — while the committed Style still owns tokens and type. Use this to make a
  pulled scene match the site, or to shift one section to a new mood. Most are
  dark. On the DOM: background→`gl-bg`, primary→`gl-ink`, secondary→
  `gl-bg-alt`/`gl-surface`, accent→`gl-accent`; use the palette's `ink` for body.
- **Fonts** (`getlayers_fonts`) — curated web typefaces, each with the exact CSS
  `stack` to write into a `gl-font-*` token, the `importUrl` to load it (Google
  Fonts, or Fontshare for General Sans), weights, and a personality note. Pass a
  font's id as `fontId` to `getlayers_materialize`, or pick display + body for a
  fresh build (see each font's `pairsWith`). A high-contrast serif display
  (Cormorant, Libre Caslon, Baskervville) is HEADLINE-ONLY — always give it a
  sturdy sans for body.

The rule that still holds: **one palette per surface, one type system per site.**
Re-dressing swaps the ramp or the face; it does not license two of either fighting
on one screen.

## The loop

For every build, in order:

1. **Interview.** First ask for as much detail as the user will give — purpose,
   audience, mood, and any references (for a 3D scene, explicitly ask for picture/
   video references). If they skip or stay vague, drive the axes as questions;
   `dimensionality` and `tone` are load-bearing — never assume them.
2. **Environment.** Establish the target. Recommend the starter; accept a refusal.
3. **Plan.** `getlayers_plan` → present Styles → **the user picks.** You do not
   pick the Style for them.
4. **Commit.** Write the choice to `getlayers.json`.
5. **Build, section by section.** Before each: re-read `getlayers.json`. After
   each: write back what you placed.

Step 5's read/write is not bureaucracy. Without it you will build section 1 in
one style and drift by section 4, because you'll have forgotten what you chose.

## How the page comes alive — read `revealChoreography`

`getlayers_start` returns a `revealChoreography` doc alongside this one. It is the
**default** for every build, not an upgrade: an immersive loader, content gated until
it completes, text and images and scroll revealing in sequence rather than simply
appearing, and any 3D scene entering with a real entrance instead of a fade.

Read it before you write the page shell, because two of its rules change your
structure rather than decorating it — the gate flips at the *start* of the curtain's
exit (so content animates in **through** the departing curtain), and everything is
mounted already-hidden rather than withheld from paint. Retrofitting either one is
much harder than building with it.

Loaders are Sections (`role: "loader"`) — browse and swap them like anything else.

Simplify it when the user asks, or when the page is a dashboard or app shell someone
opens many times a day. An immersive loader is a first-impression instrument.

## What you must not do

- Do not invent a Style. If nothing matches, say so and let the user adjust.
- Do not clone an asset wholesale into an unrelated design. Re-skin it.

**Using something as a reference.** The user can name ANY asset — a template, a
section, a scene, a background — as a reference for what to build ("make this
section like <template>"). Pull it with `getlayers_source` (or read its card),
study its composition / technique / CONFIG, then apply that to the target. Cross-type
is fine: a template can be the reference for a single section.

- Do not rewrite a `preserve` layer.
- Do not materialize speculatively. Browse is free; materialize is not.
```

## combinationRules — Règles de combinaison
```markdown
# Combination rules

What actually goes with what. These are the judgments that make the difference
between "a site built from parts" and "a site."

## Hard rules

- **One Style per site.** Never two. If a section can't be re-skinned into the
  committed Style, it's the wrong section — swap the section, not the Style.
- **`tone` never mixes — for Scenes and Backgrounds.** Their contrast is baked
  (shader constants, video), so a dark one re-skinned light turns to mud. Sections
  and Styles are different: a section's tone is just which tokens shipped, and
  repainting it to the committed Style across tone is the whole point. So a dark
  Style freely adopts a light-shipped Section; it does not adopt a light Scene.
- **One Scene above the fold. At most.** Two WebGL contexts competing for the
  first paint is the fastest way to make an expensive site feel cheap.
- **A Scene and a Background never occupy the same slot.** Pick one.

## Cost

Scenes are tagged `light` / `medium` / `heavy`.

- `heavy` above the fold is a bad trade — it delays the first meaningful paint.
  Put heavy scenes further down, and lazy-mount them.
- More than ~2 scenes on a page is almost always wrong. The rest should be
  Backgrounds or flat sections.

## Motion energy

`motionEnergy` is a page-level budget, not a per-section property. If the brief
says `subtle`, one `intense` section doesn't read as a highlight — it reads as a
mistake. Keep placed sections within one step of the brief's energy.

The exception, and it's the good one: a single `intense` moment inside an
otherwise `still` page **is** the design, when it lands on the hero and nowhere
else.

## Density and rhythm

Don't stack three `dense` sections. Alternate. `sparse → dense → sparse` reads
as rhythm; `dense → dense → dense` reads as a spreadsheet.

## Palettes (re-tinting)

- **One palette per surface.** A palette is a single hue set for a whole scene or
  section. Two palettes on one screen is the colour-layer version of two Styles on
  one site — don't. Re-tint a section to a *different* palette than its neighbour
  only for a deliberate mood break, and keep the accent family related.
- **`tone` doesn't flip — same as scenes.** A dark palette on a light-baked scene,
  or vice versa, muddies it. Re-tint within tone; the palette catalogue is mostly
  dark for exactly this reason.
- **The accent is rationed.** Every palette resolves an `accent` role — it's the
  one hot hue, not a fill. If a section reads as loud after re-tinting, the accent
  is doing too much work.
- **Palette overrides the Style for colour only.** `paletteId` re-tints; the
  committed Style still owns tokens, radius, motion, and type. Don't let a re-tint
  quietly become a second Style.

## Fonts (re-typing)

- **One type system per site.** At most a display face + a body face (+ mono if
  needed). A third family almost always reads as indecision.
- **Display-contrast serifs are headline-only.** Cormorant, Libre Caslon Display,
  and Baskervville fall apart as body text — pair each with a sturdy sans (their
  `pairsWith`). Single-weight faces build hierarchy with SIZE, not weight.
- **Match the mood, then the pairing.** Pick the face whose `mood` fits the brief,
  then let `pairsWith` choose its partner. A luxe serif display over a neutral
  sans body (e.g. Cormorant + Work Sans) is the reliable editorial move.
- **Load only the weights you use.** Every extra weight is bytes on the critical
  path. Prefer the variable fonts when you need a wide range.

## Seeding a Template from a real project

A Template is just a Style plus an ordered Section list. The fastest honest way
to get good ones is to lift them from projects that already cohere — the section
order in a shipped project *is* a proven recipe.

But: sections inside one project were tuned together. Lifting the *order* is
safe. Lifting the *sections* into a different Style needs each one re-skinned,
and that's what the contract is for.
```

## revealChoreography — Chorégraphie de révélation
```markdown
# Reveal choreography — the house default

Every ODORO build gets this **by default**. A user can ask for it simplified or dropped; you
do not need permission to include it.

    immersive loader  →  gate  →  staggered content reveal  →  scene reveal

These rules were harvested from 11 templates, not invented. Where a number appears, it is a real
number from a shipped template. Where templates disagree, the disagreement is noted and a default
is chosen — with the reason.

---

## 1. The loader

**Be honest about what you are measuring, or don't show a number.**

Three legitimate designs, in descending order of preference:

**A. Asset-backed with a holding ceiling.** The counter tracks real readiness and *parks* short of
100 until the thing it's waiting for arrives.

    dt = min((now - last)/1000, 0.05)
    if (ready && v >= 99.4) v = 100                    // snap the last 0.6%
    else { ceiling = ready ? 100 : 92
           v += (ceiling - v) * (ready ? 6 : 1.7) * dt }

Two rates: a slow crawl toward a **92%** holding ceiling while loading, a fast run to 100 once
ready. If the asset stalls, the bar sits at 92 forever — which is honest. `altitude` does the same
with a 90 ceiling and two springs, and notes the ceiling is *a target, not a milestone*: on a warm
cache the interrupt lands at ~54, never touching 90.

**B. No counter at all.** A wordmark, a hairline, a veil. `halcyon` counts nothing and is the most
expensive-feeling loader in the library. `baseline`'s bar is a **timer, not a readout** — 1280ms
of `scaleX` timed to land flush with the end of the minimum-visible window. If you are not
measuring anything, do not draw a percentage.

**C. Paced curtain.** A fixed clock, honestly fixed. `artist` runs 0→100 over exactly 1500ms with
`1-(1-p)³` applied **to the number itself**, not to a CSS transition, so it decelerates into 100.

**Never** show a percentage that is a `setTimeout` dressed as progress.

### Always
- **`MIN_VISIBLE`** — 900–1600ms anti-flash floor, so a warm cache doesn't flash a curtain.
  (`forma` 900, `baseline` 1400, `altitude` 1300, `halcyon` 1600.)
- **A hard cap** — 2600–7000ms, so a stalled asset can never trap the visitor.
  (`baseline` 2600, `forma` 7000, `halcyon` 7000.)
- **"Ready" means ≥1 drawn frame.** Both templates that gate on WebGL fire `onReady` from *inside*
  the rAF loop, after the first `renderer.render` — so "ready" implies the shader compiled and the
  GPU drew. Resolving a promise is not readiness.

---

## 2. The gate

**Flip the gate at the START of the exit, never on its rest.** This is the single most consistent
finding in the library — `neural-monitor`, `forma`, `baseline`, `artist`, `halcyon`, `altitude`
and `marcus-vane` all do it, and the two that don't were judged worse by the people who read them.

The point is overlap. The content must animate in *through* the departing curtain:
- `marcus-vane` doesn't even use a callback — the hero runs on an absolute 2500ms clock, by which
  point the curtain is only **75% lifted**, so the wordmark rises behind the last quarter of the
  plate and the two moves read as one gesture.
- `halcyon` starts the copy while the veil is still **~40% opaque** and the camera entrance is
  mid-flight. Its porting agent shipped the "wait for rest" version first, saw it, and fixed it.
- `altitude` flips at 100 *before* the aperture starts opening, so the page animates in through the
  hole.

**Gate by holding state, not by withholding paint.** Mount everything at first paint and let it
sit at its `from` value. Reasons, all found in the wild:
- Crawlers and screen readers see the content (`altitude` keeps `spring-text-engine`'s hidden `seo`
  copy in the DOM).
- Text measuring and splitting happen behind the curtain, so the reveal is a cheap opacity/transform
  with no remount and cannot stall the frame (`flowstate`).
- Mounting late seeds scroll progress from a zero-height document and snaps a scroll-driven scene
  to its finale (`neural-monitor`).

Prefer `enabled={ready}` passed to each leaf over a global class. If an element must replay from
zero, force a remount with `key={ready ? 'on' : 'off'}` (`baseline`, `lumora`).

**Scroll release is separate from the visual gate.** Lock scroll on loader mount; release it on
the curtain's `onRest` — later than the content reveal, and that's correct.

---

## 3. Content reveal

**Per word or per line. Per character is for short display type only** — a wordmark, a hero line.
Never a paragraph.

Typical, from the library:

| unit | stagger | duration | used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| line | 90–140ms | 900–1100ms | `baseline`, `lumora`, `artist`, `gravity-webgl` |
| word | 20–85ms | 520–900ms | `flowstate` 85, `forma` 52, `halcyon` 75, `lumora` 35, `artist` 22 |
| char | 20–70ms | 720–950ms | `forma` 20, `altitude` 26, `marcus-vane` 52, `loopstack` 90 |

**Non-negotiable details, each learned the hard way:**

- **Protect descenders.** A clipped line mask crops descenders. Every template that clips adds
  `padding-bottom: .12–.15em; margin-bottom: -.12–-.15em`.
- **Never clip a blurred reveal.** `overflow` shears the blur halo at the line box — which is the
  entire point of the effect. `altitude` and `forma` found this independently.
- **Land opacity early in the curve.** `loopstack` hits full opacity at 25–30% of the timing
  function, so the type is *solid while still travelling and de-blurring*. That, not the translate,
  is what makes it read expensive.
- **One text engine per designed line.** One engine for a whole sentence re-wraps it — its
  container measures differently from a paragraph — and two designed lines come out as three.
  Continue the second engine's delay from the first's count so it still reads as one sweep.
- **Reveal in place when there's a scene behind.** `halcyon` uses opacity + blur with **no
  translate**, so words materialise without shifting over moving water.

**Below the fold is a different mechanic.** Gate only above-the-fold content on the loader;
everything else is plain viewport-entry, `once`, latching at 45–88% visible. Don't gate what
nobody can see.

---

## 4. Scroll

**One clock. One quantisation.** Lenis (or equivalent) drives a single normalised progress value;
everything reads from it.

- Write progress to a **ref**, not state, and read it imperatively inside the frame loop —
  scrolling must never re-render the tree.
- If DOM chrome needs discrete stages, quantise **from the same value** the scene uses.
  `neural-monitor` ships a genuine bug here: the camera uses `progress × 6` legs while the chrome
  uses `floor(progress × 7)` bands, so its takeover cover fades in ~29vh before its panel is framed.
- **Align keyframes to panel boundaries.** With N full-viewport panels, spread progress over N−1
  legs so keyframe *i* lands exactly when panel *i* fills the viewport. One panel of scrolling =
  one leg. `neural-monitor`'s camera is good almost entirely because of this.

Most reveals should be **viewport-entry**, not scroll-scrubbed. Scrub only what genuinely benefits:
a parallax plate, a counter, a camera. `lumora` scrubs exactly one thing (stat counters, which
count back down on scroll-up); `artist` scrubs two; `baseline` two.

---

## 5. The scene

**A 3D scene never fades in as a whole object.** Give it a physical entrance:

- **Full brightness on frame 0, then hand off.** `flowstate` detonates 34 ink splats at mount —
  the very first painted frame is peak brightness, no ramp — then re-ignites for 8 frames, then an
  invisible auto-cursor takes over at 700ms and orbits forever. Dye decays at 0.958/step, so the
  burst drains exactly across the content stagger. **Tune the content stagger so its midpoint sits
  in the decay valley between the burst and the ambient driver.** The scene never has a dead moment
  and the content never lands on a static ground.
- **Fly it in.** `gravity-webgl` parks 96 spheres off-screen with zero velocity, then on
  loader-complete re-scatters them inward with an `attractionBoost` of `lerp(7.5, 1, easeOutCubic(t/2.2))`
  — a 2.2s hard pull relaxing into the ambient spring. `neural-monitor` flies its brain in from
  `z 3.6 → 0` while unwinding a full `2π` turn, alpha 0→1, **all three on one shared eased scalar**
  so it lands as one gesture rather than three overlapping ones.
- **Dissolve, don't fade.** `halcyon` reveals through a 3D-noise dissolve band with an edge glow,
  and drops the camera from high above the sea to skimming it over 2.8s, out of a white-out.

**Interpolate linearly and damp once.** Do not hand-ease every segment. One frame-rate-independent
damp gives the whole thing weight:

    const k = 1 - Math.exp(-DAMP * Math.min(delta, 0.1))
    camera.position.lerp(target.position, k)
    lookAt.lerp(target.lookAt, k)          // damp separately, then camera.lookAt(lookAt)

`DAMP = 3.2` → τ ≈ 312ms, 95% settle ≈ 940ms. **That lag is the weight** — the camera sits a third
of a second behind your scroll, which is what makes it read as flown rather than scrubbed. Clamp
`delta` so a tab-restore can't teleport. Damp position and look-at as separate vectors so the
framing swings instead of pivoting rigidly. Pass **real `delta`** — a hardcoded `1/60` converges
twice as fast on a 120Hz display.

**Frame with the look-at, not the model.** A negative `target.x` puts the subject off-centre and
leaves the other half for copy, without moving the object.

**Shader uniforms usually should NOT be damped** — a soft falloff reads smooth on raw linear
values, and the camera's own damping already softens the apparent motion.

---

## 6. Reduced motion

`prefers-reduced-motion` must reach **everything**, and this is where the library is weakest.

The clean pattern: toggle the animation library's global skip (`skipAnimation` in react-spring) so
every spring jumps to its end state, loader included — `forma`, `baseline` and `flowstate` do this.

**But two templates ship a real bug you must not copy:** `flowstate`'s shader ignores the setting
and keeps running; `neural-monitor` pins its camera at progress 0 while the scene keeps scanning
regions and exploding at the finale — a frozen camera watching an animated brain. A canvas or
shader loop is not covered by your animation library's global flag. Turn it off yourself.

Reduce, don't delete: `gravity-webgl` drops translate and blur under reduced motion and **keeps
opacity**, so the page still resolves rather than snapping.

---

## When to simplify

Drop it to a plain fade — or nothing — when the user asks, or when the page is a dashboard, an app
shell, or anything a person will visit many times a day. An immersive loader is for a page someone
sees once and should remember. It is a first-impression instrument, not a habit.
```

The\nfailure it prevents is specific and common: an agent re-skins a section, quietly\n\"tidies\" the animation timing, and ships something that no longer feels designed.\n\n## The one insight that makes mixing work\n\nTwo sections from different origins clash **only in the skin layer.** Their\ncomposition and motion are fully portable.\n\nSo page coherence does **not** come from sections sharing a source. It comes from\nthem sharing **one Style, applied at assembly time.** Pull section A, pull section\nB, paint both with the committed Style's tokens → they cohere despite different\norigins.\n\nThis is why the Style is committed **once, early, and never drifts.** It is the\nsingle most important decision in the build. Get it from the user explicitly.\n\n## Colour on a 3D Scene is a parameter, never code\n\nA Scene exposes its entire art-direction surface as `CONFIG` — typically 20–50\nnamed knobs, colours as `#rrggbb`. `materialize` hands you a `tint` map that\nresolves the committed Style's palette onto that scene's own colour keys.\n\n**Apply the tint to CONFIG. Never edit the shader to recolour.** Shaders are not\nre-tintable by editing — you will produce garbage. If a colour you want isn't in\nCONFIG, it isn't available. Say so; don't go hunting in the GLSL.\n\nNote also: params marked `structural: true` rebuild geometry. Most scenes need a\nreload for those; only a few rebuild live.\n\n## Every page is compositions + a Style + assets\n\nThis is the model. A **composition** is a section's layout skeleton (an abstract\nwireframe: where headline, media, model, buttons, nav sit; their relative sizes;\nthe white space) — no fonts, colours, copy, or assets. The **Style** is the skin.\nThe **assets** are the organs. A template is just a fixed set of compositions with\na style and assets already chosen.\n\nSo there are two ways to build, and compositions are central to both:\n\n- **Extending a template** — materialize it and re-skin. Each section reports its\n  `composition` and `recomposeOptions`. To *restructure* a section (not just\n  recolour it), swap its composition for another of the same role and rebuild that\n  section to the new skeleton, keeping the Style and content. That is how a user\n  changes a hero from one layout to another without leaving the template.\n- **Building a section from scratch** — call `getlayers_compositions` (by role)\n  FIRST, pick a skeleton, and pour the committed Style + chosen assets into its\n  slots. Honour its type scale, spacing, and balance. Combine skeletons down the\n  page for rhythm (`pairsWith`). NEVER default to a generic centered stack — that\n  is the single most common failure.\n\n## Re-dressing: palettes and fonts\n\nTwo reference catalogues (like compositions, they ship no source) let you\n**re-dress** any asset — swap its colour or its type without touching composition\nor motion:\n\n- **Palettes** (`getlayers_palettes`) — portable colour ramps. Each resolves the\n  same four roles a Style does (background / primary / secondary / accent), so it\n  drops straight into the tint pipeline. Pass a palette's id as `paletteId` to\n  `getlayers_materialize` and the scene comes back tinted to it *instead of* the\n  Style — while the committed Style still owns tokens and type. Use this to make a\n  pulled scene match the site, or to shift one section to a new mood. Most are\n  dark. On the DOM: background→`gl-bg`, primary→`gl-ink`, secondary→\n  `gl-bg-alt`/`gl-surface`, accent→`gl-accent`; use the palette's `ink` for body.\n- **Fonts** (`getlayers_fonts`) — curated web typefaces, each with the exact CSS\n  `stack` to write into a `gl-font-*` token, the `importUrl` to load it (Google\n  Fonts, or Fontshare for General Sans), weights, and a personality note. Pass a\n  font's id as `fontId` to `getlayers_materialize`, or pick display + body for a\n  fresh build (see each font's `pairsWith`). A high-contrast serif display\n  (Cormorant, Libre Caslon, Baskervville) is HEADLINE-ONLY — always give it a\n  sturdy sans for body.\n\nThe rule that still holds: **one palette per surface, one type system per site.**\nRe-dressing swaps the ramp or the face; it does not license two of either fighting\non one screen.\n\n## The loop\n\nFor every build, in order:\n\n1. **Interview.** First ask for as much detail as the user will give — purpose,\n   audience, mood, and any references (for a 3D scene, explicitly ask for picture/\n   video references). If they skip or stay vague, drive the axes as questions;\n   `dimensionality` and `tone` are load-bearing — never assume them.\n2. **Environment.** Establish the target. Recommend the starter; accept a refusal.\n3. **Plan.** `getlayers_plan` → present Styles → **the user picks.** You do not\n   pick the Style for them.\n4. **Commit.** Write the choice to `getlayers.json`.\n5. **Build, section by section.** Before each: re-read `getlayers.json`. After\n   each: write back what you placed.\n\nStep 5's read/write is not bureaucracy. Without it you will build section 1 in\none style and drift by section 4, because you'll have forgotten what you chose.\n\n## How the page comes alive — read `revealChoreography`\n\n`getlayers_start` returns a `revealChoreography` doc alongside this one. It is the\n**default** for every build, not an upgrade: an immersive loader, content gated until\nit completes, text and images and scroll revealing in sequence rather than simply\nappearing, and any 3D scene entering with a real entrance instead of a fade.\n\nRead it before you write the page shell, because two of its rules change your\nstructure rather than decorating it — the gate flips at the *start* of the curtain's\nexit (so content animates in **through** the departing curtain), and everything is\nmounted already-hidden rather than withheld from paint. Retrofitting either one is\nmuch harder than building with it.\n\nLoaders are Sections (`role: \"loader\"`) — browse and swap them like anything else.\n\nSimplify it when the user asks, or when the page is a dashboard or app shell someone\nopens many times a day. An immersive loader is a first-impression instrument.\n\n## What you must not do\n\n- Do not invent a Style. If nothing matches, say so and let the user adjust.\n- Do not clone an asset wholesale into an unrelated design. Re-skin it.\n\n**Using something as a reference.** The user can name ANY asset — a template, a\nsection, a scene, a background — as a reference for what to build (\"make this\nsection like <template>\"). Pull it with `getlayers_source` (or read its card),\nstudy its composition / technique / CONFIG, then apply that to the target. Cross-type\nis fine: a template can be the reference for a single section.\n\n- Do not rewrite a `preserve` layer.\n- Do not materialize speculatively. Browse is free; materialize is not.\n",
  "combinationRules": "# Combination rules\n\nWhat actually goes with what. These are the judgments that make the difference\nbetween \"a site built from parts\" and \"a site.\"\n\n## Hard rules\n\n- **One Style per site.** Never two. If a section can't be re-skinned into the\n  committed Style, it's the wrong section — swap the section, not the Style.\n- **`tone` never mixes — for Scenes and Backgrounds.** Their contrast is baked\n  (shader constants, video), so a dark one re-skinned light turns to mud. Sections\n  and Styles are different: a section's tone is just which tokens shipped, and\n  repainting it to the committed Style across tone is the whole point. So a dark\n  Style freely adopts a light-shipped Section; it does not adopt a light Scene.\n- **One Scene above the fold. At most.** Two WebGL contexts competing for the\n  first paint is the fastest way to make an expensive site feel cheap.\n- **A Scene and a Background never occupy the same slot.** Pick one.\n\n## Cost\n\nScenes are tagged `light` / `medium` / `heavy`.\n\n- `heavy` above the fold is a bad trade — it delays the first meaningful paint.\n  Put heavy scenes further down, and lazy-mount them.\n- More than ~2 scenes on a page is almost always wrong. The rest should be\n  Backgrounds or flat sections.\n\n## Motion energy\n\n`motionEnergy` is a page-level budget, not a per-section property. If the brief\nsays `subtle`, one `intense` section doesn't read as a highlight — it reads as a\nmistake. Keep placed sections within one step of the brief's energy.\n\nThe exception, and it's the good one: a single `intense` moment inside an\notherwise `still` page **is** the design, when it lands on the hero and nowhere\nelse.\n\n## Density and rhythm\n\nDon't stack three `dense` sections. Alternate. `sparse → dense → sparse` reads\nas rhythm; `dense → dense → dense` reads as a spreadsheet.\n\n## Palettes (re-tinting)\n\n- **One palette per surface.** A palette is a single hue set for a whole scene or\n  section. Two palettes on one screen is the colour-layer version of two Styles on\n  one site — don't. Re-tint a section to a *different* palette than its neighbour\n  only for a deliberate mood break, and keep the accent family related.\n- **`tone` doesn't flip — same as scenes.** A dark palette on a light-baked scene,\n  or vice versa, muddies it. Re-tint within tone; the palette catalogue is mostly\n  dark for exactly this reason.\n- **The accent is rationed.** Every palette resolves an `accent` role — it's the\n  one hot hue, not a fill. If a section reads as loud after re-tinting, the accent\n  is doing too much work.\n- **Palette overrides the Style for colour only.** `paletteId` re-tints; the\n  committed Style still owns tokens, radius, motion, and type. Don't let a re-tint\n  quietly become a second Style.\n\n## Fonts (re-typing)\n\n- **One type system per site.** At most a display face + a body face (+ mono if\n  needed). A third family almost always reads as indecision.\n- **Display-contrast serifs are headline-only.** Cormorant, Libre Caslon Display,\n  and Baskervville fall apart as body text — pair each with a sturdy sans (their\n  `pairsWith`). Single-weight faces build hierarchy with SIZE, not weight.\n- **Match the mood, then the pairing.** Pick the face whose `mood` fits the brief,\n  then let `pairsWith` choose its partner. A luxe serif display over a neutral\n  sans body (e.g. Cormorant + Work Sans) is the reliable editorial move.\n- **Load only the weights you use.** Every extra weight is bytes on the critical\n  path. Prefer the variable fonts when you need a wide range.\n\n## Seeding a Template from a real project\n\nA Template is just a Style plus an ordered Section list. The fastest honest way\nto get good ones is to lift them from projects that already cohere — the section\norder in a shipped project *is* a proven recipe.\n\nBut: sections inside one project were tuned together. Lifting the *order* is\nsafe. Lifting the *sections* into a different Style needs each one re-skinned,\nand that's what the contract is for.\n",
  "revealChoreography": "# Reveal choreography — the house default\n\nEvery ODORO build gets this **by default**. A user can ask for it simplified or dropped; you\ndo not need permission to include it.\n\n    immersive loader  →  gate  →  staggered content reveal  →  scene reveal\n\nThese rules were harvested from 11 templates, not invented. Where a number appears, it is a real\nnumber from a shipped template. Where templates disagree, the disagreement is noted and a default\nis chosen — with the reason.\n\n---\n\n## 1. The loader\n\n**Be honest about what you are measuring, or don't show a number.**\n\nThree legitimate designs, in descending order of preference:\n\n**A. Asset-backed with a holding ceiling.** The counter tracks real readiness and *parks* short of\n100 until the thing it's waiting for arrives.\n\n    dt = min((now - last)/1000, 0.05)\n    if (ready && v >= 99.4) v = 100                    // snap the last 0.6%\n    else { ceiling = ready ? 100 : 92\n           v += (ceiling - v) * (ready ? 6 : 1.7) * dt }\n\nTwo rates: a slow crawl toward a **92%** holding ceiling while loading, a fast run to 100 once\nready. If the asset stalls, the bar sits at 92 forever — which is honest. `altitude` does the same\nwith a 90 ceiling and two springs, and notes the ceiling is *a target, not a milestone*: on a warm\ncache the interrupt lands at ~54, never touching 90.\n\n**B. No counter at all.** A wordmark, a hairline, a veil. `halcyon` counts nothing and is the most\nexpensive-feeling loader in the library. `baseline`'s bar is a **timer, not a readout** — 1280ms\nof `scaleX` timed to land flush with the end of the minimum-visible window. If you are not\nmeasuring anything, do not draw a percentage.\n\n**C. Paced curtain.** A fixed clock, honestly fixed. `artist` runs 0→100 over exactly 1500ms with\n`1-(1-p)³` applied **to the number itself**, not to a CSS transition, so it decelerates into 100.\n\n**Never** show a percentage that is a `setTimeout` dressed as progress.\n\n### Always\n- **`MIN_VISIBLE`** — 900–1600ms anti-flash floor, so a warm cache doesn't flash a curtain.\n  (`forma` 900, `baseline` 1400, `altitude` 1300, `halcyon` 1600.)\n- **A hard cap** — 2600–7000ms, so a stalled asset can never trap the visitor.\n  (`baseline` 2600, `forma` 7000, `halcyon` 7000.)\n- **\"Ready\" means ≥1 drawn frame.** Both templates that gate on WebGL fire `onReady` from *inside*\n  the rAF loop, after the first `renderer.render` — so \"ready\" implies the shader compiled and the\n  GPU drew. Resolving a promise is not readiness.\n\n---\n\n## 2. The gate\n\n**Flip the gate at the START of the exit, never on its rest.** This is the single most consistent\nfinding in the library — `neural-monitor`, `forma`, `baseline`, `artist`, `halcyon`, `altitude`\nand `marcus-vane` all do it, and the two that don't were judged worse by the people who read them.\n\nThe point is overlap. The content must animate in *through* the departing curtain:\n- `marcus-vane` doesn't even use a callback — the hero runs on an absolute 2500ms clock, by which\n  point the curtain is only **75% lifted**, so the wordmark rises behind the last quarter of the\n  plate and the two moves read as one gesture.\n- `halcyon` starts the copy while the veil is still **~40% opaque** and the camera entrance is\n  mid-flight. Its porting agent shipped the \"wait for rest\" version first, saw it, and fixed it.\n- `altitude` flips at 100 *before* the aperture starts opening, so the page animates in through the\n  hole.\n\n**Gate by holding state, not by withholding paint.** Mount everything at first paint and let it\nsit at its `from` value. Reasons, all found in the wild:\n- Crawlers and screen readers see the content (`altitude` keeps `spring-text-engine`'s hidden `seo`\n  copy in the DOM).\n- Text measuring and splitting happen behind the curtain, so the reveal is a cheap opacity/transform\n  with no remount and cannot stall the frame (`flowstate`).\n- Mounting late seeds scroll progress from a zero-height document and snaps a scroll-driven scene\n  to its finale (`neural-monitor`).\n\nPrefer `enabled={ready}` passed to each leaf over a global class. If an element must replay from\nzero, force a remount with `key={ready ? 'on' : 'off'}` (`baseline`, `lumora`).\n\n**Scroll release is separate from the visual gate.** Lock scroll on loader mount; release it on\nthe curtain's `onRest` — later than the content reveal, and that's correct.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Content reveal\n\n**Per word or per line. Per character is for short display type only** — a wordmark, a hero line.\nNever a paragraph.\n\nTypical, from the library:\n\n| unit | stagger | duration | used by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| line | 90–140ms | 900–1100ms | `baseline`, `lumora`, `artist`, `gravity-webgl` |\n| word | 20–85ms | 520–900ms | `flowstate` 85, `forma` 52, `halcyon` 75, `lumora` 35, `artist` 22 |\n| char | 20–70ms | 720–950ms | `forma` 20, `altitude` 26, `marcus-vane` 52, `loopstack` 90 |\n\n**Non-negotiable details, each learned the hard way:**\n\n- **Protect descenders.** A clipped line mask crops descenders. Every template that clips adds\n  `padding-bottom: .12–.15em; margin-bottom: -.12–-.15em`.\n- **Never clip a blurred reveal.** `overflow` shears the blur halo at the line box — which is the\n  entire point of the effect. `altitude` and `forma` found this independently.\n- **Land opacity early in the curve.** `loopstack` hits full opacity at 25–30% of the timing\n  function, so the type is *solid while still travelling and de-blurring*. That, not the translate,\n  is what makes it read expensive.\n- **One text engine per designed line.** One engine for a whole sentence re-wraps it — its\n  container measures differently from a paragraph — and two designed lines come out as three.\n  Continue the second engine's delay from the first's count so it still reads as one sweep.\n- **Reveal in place when there's a scene behind.** `halcyon` uses opacity + blur with **no\n  translate**, so words materialise without shifting over moving water.\n\n**Below the fold is a different mechanic.** Gate only above-the-fold content on the loader;\neverything else is plain viewport-entry, `once`, latching at 45–88% visible. Don't gate what\nnobody can see.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Scroll\n\n**One clock. One quantisation.** Lenis (or equivalent) drives a single normalised progress value;\neverything reads from it.\n\n- Write progress to a **ref**, not state, and read it imperatively inside the frame loop —\n  scrolling must never re-render the tree.\n- If DOM chrome needs discrete stages, quantise **from the same value** the scene uses.\n  `neural-monitor` ships a genuine bug here: the camera uses `progress × 6` legs while the chrome\n  uses `floor(progress × 7)` bands, so its takeover cover fades in ~29vh before its panel is framed.\n- **Align keyframes to panel boundaries.** With N full-viewport panels, spread progress over N−1\n  legs so keyframe *i* lands exactly when panel *i* fills the viewport. One panel of scrolling =\n  one leg. `neural-monitor`'s camera is good almost entirely because of this.\n\nMost reveals should be **viewport-entry**, not scroll-scrubbed. Scrub only what genuinely benefits:\na parallax plate, a counter, a camera. `lumora` scrubs exactly one thing (stat counters, which\ncount back down on scroll-up); `artist` scrubs two; `baseline` two.\n\n---\n\n## 5. The scene\n\n**A 3D scene never fades in as a whole object.** Give it a physical entrance:\n\n- **Full brightness on frame 0, then hand off.** `flowstate` detonates 34 ink splats at mount —\n  the very first painted frame is peak brightness, no ramp — then re-ignites for 8 frames, then an\n  invisible auto-cursor takes over at 700ms and orbits forever. Dye decays at 0.958/step, so the\n  burst drains exactly across the content stagger. **Tune the content stagger so its midpoint sits\n  in the decay valley between the burst and the ambient driver.** The scene never has a dead moment\n  and the content never lands on a static ground.\n- **Fly it in.** `gravity-webgl` parks 96 spheres off-screen with zero velocity, then on\n  loader-complete re-scatters them inward with an `attractionBoost` of `lerp(7.5, 1, easeOutCubic(t/2.2))`\n  — a 2.2s hard pull relaxing into the ambient spring. `neural-monitor` flies its brain in from\n  `z 3.6 → 0` while unwinding a full `2π` turn, alpha 0→1, **all three on one shared eased scalar**\n  so it lands as one gesture rather than three overlapping ones.\n- **Dissolve, don't fade.** `halcyon` reveals through a 3D-noise dissolve band with an edge glow,\n  and drops the camera from high above the sea to skimming it over 2.8s, out of a white-out.\n\n**Interpolate linearly and damp once.** Do not hand-ease every segment. One frame-rate-independent\ndamp gives the whole thing weight:\n\n    const k = 1 - Math.exp(-DAMP * Math.min(delta, 0.1))\n    camera.position.lerp(target.position, k)\n    lookAt.lerp(target.lookAt, k)          // damp separately, then camera.lookAt(lookAt)\n\n`DAMP = 3.2` → τ ≈ 312ms, 95% settle ≈ 940ms. **That lag is the weight** — the camera sits a third\nof a second behind your scroll, which is what makes it read as flown rather than scrubbed. Clamp\n`delta` so a tab-restore can't teleport. Damp position and look-at as separate vectors so the\nframing swings instead of pivoting rigidly. Pass **real `delta`** — a hardcoded `1/60` converges\ntwice as fast on a 120Hz display.\n\n**Frame with the look-at, not the model.** A negative `target.x` puts the subject off-centre and\nleaves the other half for copy, without moving the object.\n\n**Shader uniforms usually should NOT be damped** — a soft falloff reads smooth on raw linear\nvalues, and the camera's own damping already softens the apparent motion.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Reduced motion\n\n`prefers-reduced-motion` must reach **everything**, and this is where the library is weakest.\n\nThe clean pattern: toggle the animation library's global skip (`skipAnimation` in react-spring) so\nevery spring jumps to its end state, loader included — `forma`, `baseline` and `flowstate` do this.\n\n**But two templates ship a real bug you must not copy:** `flowstate`'s shader ignores the setting\nand keeps running; `neural-monitor` pins its camera at progress 0 while the scene keeps scanning\nregions and exploding at the finale — a frozen camera watching an animated brain. A canvas or\nshader loop is not covered by your animation library's global flag. Turn it off yourself.\n\nReduce, don't delete: `gravity-webgl` drops translate and blur under reduced motion and **keeps\nopacity**, so the page still resolves rather than snapping.\n\n---\n\n## When to simplify\n\nDrop it to a plain fade — or nothing — when the user asks, or when the page is a dashboard, an app\nshell, or anything a person will visit many times a day. An immersive loader is for a page someone\nsees once and should remember. It is a first-impression instrument, not a habit.\n",

# 5. getlayers_state_schema — getlayers.json
````markdown
# `getlayers.json` — the project state

Lives in the user's repo root. **Typed, not prose.** Prose drifts and bloats over
a long build; a schema stays queryable and lets every MCP call be primed exactly.

Read it before every section you build. Write to it after every section you place.

```jsonc
{
  "version": 1,

  // What the user asked for, normalised onto the axes. Set once, after the interview.
  "brief": {
    "dimensionality": ["3d"],
    "mood": ["luxe"],
    "tone": ["dark"],
    "motionEnergy": ["subtle"],
    "density": ["sparse"]
  },

  // The committed Style. THE load-bearing decision. Set once; changing it means
  // re-skinning everything already placed.
  "styleId": "obsidian-luxe",

  // Resolved token values — the Style's, plus any user overrides. This is what
  // every section is painted with. Canonical --gl-* names only.
  "tokens": {
    "gl-bg": "#0a0a0c",
    "gl-ink": "#f4f4f5",
    "gl-accent": "#c9a227"
  },

  "activeTemplateId": "obsidian-luxe-agency",

  // Everything built so far, in page order.
  "placed": [
    {
      "sectionId": "hero-mirror-hall",
      "slot": 0,
      "sceneId": "aether-flux",
      // Any CONFIG overrides applied to the scene in THIS placement.
      "sceneParams": { "silverWarm": "#c9a227", "flowSpeed": 0.18 }
    },
    { "sectionId": "showcase-equator", "slot": 1 }
  ],

  // The only place freeform notes are allowed.
  "notes": "Client rejected the first gold; second pass is cooler and less brassy."
}
```

## Why this exists

The failure it prevents: you build section 1 in one style, and by section 4 you've
forgotten what you chose and the page quietly stops cohering. The user won't be
able to name what's wrong — it'll just feel like a template.

Server = the space of good design decisions (the menu).
Client = the record of what this project already ordered.

Neither does the job alone.
````

# 6. getlayers_scene_lab — guide de création de scènes 3D
Appel : `{"description": "A calm, luxurious architectural 3D scene: warm golden light raking across sculpted concrete volumes, slow drifting camera, subtle dust in light beams", "count": 1}`

## instruction
Author a NEW self-contained single-HTML scene for this brief. Study the references below for TECHNIQUE and calibration (the CONFIG contract, shader approach, sensible ranges) — combine and adapt, do not clone any one. Honour the user's description and any reference images they shared for palette, density, and mood. Follow the guide.

## guide
````markdown
# Scene Lab — authoring a NEW 3D scene

You are building an original scene, inspired by the user's brief + reference
images + our reference scenes. Synthesise; do not clone. The references are for
technique and calibration, not to copy verbatim.

## The output

One self-contained `.html` file. Vanilla three.js via a pinned CDN importmap. No
build step. It must open and animate with no errors.

## The house contract (follow it — it's why scenes are re-skinnable)

Every tweakable value lives in ONE object, `CONFIG`, near the top:

```js
const CONFIG = {
  mainColor: '#46f5a0',   // colours are '#rrggbb' STRINGS
  density:   600,         // everything else is a NUMBER
  flowSpeed: 0.22,
}
```

- **Colours are `#rrggbb` strings; every other param is a number.** Nothing else.
- **Hoist every magic number you might want to art-direct into CONFIG.** The more
  live knobs, the more the look can be found by hand and the more re-skinnable it is.
- `applyConfig()` pushes CONFIG into the live uniforms (`.copy(hexToVec3(...))` for
  vec3 colours). Call it once at start and on every change.
- Colour a scene by editing CONFIG — NEVER by editing the shader. A shader edit to
  recolour produces garbage.

## The anatomy (shared, stable — spend your effort on the Scene class)

1. HTML head + canvas + panel CSS
2. importmap + imports (EffectComposer, RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass, ShaderPass…)
3. `const CONFIG = {…}`
4. Shared rig: DEFAULTS/localStorage, `hexToVec3()`, composers, renderer/scene/camera
5. **The `Scene` class** — the only bespoke part. Contract: `constructor(scene)`,
   `resize()`, `render()`.
6. Wiring: `applyConfig()`, resize, render loop
7. Optional dev panel: reflect over CONFIG keys → `#rrggbb` → colour input, number
   → range slider.

Sections 1–4, 6, 7 are chrome you can lift from any reference scene. Section 5 is
where the idea lives.

## Working from references

- `getlayers_scene_lab` hands you the closest scenes with their full source + the
  extracted CONFIG (`params.json`). Read them for: how the effect is built, which
  knobs matter, sensible ranges, the palette-role mapping.
- Combine techniques across references. A curl-noise field from one, a bloom
  treatment from another, a palette from the user's screenshot.
- Honour the user's reference images for palette, density, and mood. Match the
  feeling, not any one scene.

## Structural vs live

Params that change geometry (counts) usually need a rebuild — most scenes reload;
a few rebuild live. If you promise a live count slider, wire a `rebuild()`.

## Done check

Self-contained, opens clean, animates. CONFIG holds every colour (as `#rrggbb`)
and every art-direction number. Reads as the user's idea, not a copy of a
reference.
````

### source

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>

<title>Scene · Crimson Contour</title>
<style>
  html, body { margin: 0; padding: 0; height: 100%; background: #000; overflow: hidden; }

  /* UI PANEL — remove this block to drop the controls */

    border-radius: 6px; backdrop-filter: blur(10px); -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(10px);

  #ui-body input[type=range] { width: 110px; }

    border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.18); border-radius: 4px; padding: 5px 6px; font: 11px/1 sans-serif; }
